slides.headline: How strong is your grip, really?
slides.sub: It's about more than opening jars. Here's how to train it.

slides.title: More than a party trick
slides.body: Research suggests grip strength is linked with overall strength and how well people manage everyday life as they age. It isn't the whole story, but it's a handy, simple marker.

slides.title: Everyday signs to notice
slides.body: Struggling with jar lids, carrying shopping bags or holding a heavy pan can hint that your grip could use some work. Many people only notice when a task starts to feel hard.

slides.title: Carry things on purpose
slides.body: Farmer's carries are simple: hold a heavy bag or dumbbell in each hand and walk for 30 seconds. Shopping bags from the car count too, if you stand tall and take your time.

slides.title: Squeeze, pinch and hang
slides.body: Squeeze a soft ball or rolled towel, pinch two weight plates together, or hang briefly from a bar with your feet on the ground. Two or three times a week is plenty.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Weakness in one hand, pins and needles, dropping things more often, or swollen, painful finger joints are all worth a proper assessment rather than more squeezing at home.

caption:
When did you last think about your grip?

Research suggests grip strength is linked with overall strength and how well people manage as they get older. It's a small, simple marker, and one of the easiest things to train.

Try farmer's carries with shopping bags or dumbbells, squeeze a soft ball while you watch TV, or hang briefly from a bar with your feet on the ground. Two or three short sessions a week is plenty. If one hand is weaker, tingly or dropping things, get that checked first.
